callout.text: Not a list of pros and cons

explainedBy: Mechanism step one: instead of pros and cons, you write out your core values — the first step of a flow the next beats build.

storyboard.claim: Linear value modeling starts by listing core values, not pros and cons.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow diagram opens with its first step: List core values.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the walk-through promised in 302.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the method as a sequence of steps, step one drawn.

explainedBy: Mechanism step two: each listed value gets a weight from 0 to 1 — the flow gains its second step.

storyboard.claim: Each value is given a weight from 0 to 1 by importance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same flow, now with a second step: Weight each 0 to 1.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept flow; one step added.
storyboard.addedInformation: The weighting range from the narration.

explainedBy: Reaction: the listener, holding the sheet of values, is struck that this means grading his soul — weather and friendships each get a number.
noVisual: A reaction to the method; the held sheet carries the values, the face carries the surprise.

storyboard.claim: The host reacts: this is grading our soul, giving weather and friendship a weight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener holds a sheet of notes, surprised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the method diagram to a person reacting to it.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the surprise is the reaction; the values themselves come next.

explainedBy: Johnson's own weight: nature and weather get 0.4 — nice but not existential; the first bucket of the couple's value sheet.

storyboard.claim: Steven weights nature and good weather at 0.4.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter with one bucket: Nature and weather: 0.4.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the method to the couple's actual numbers.
storyboard.addedInformation: The specific weight from the narration.

explainedBy: His wife's weight: daily nearness to close friends gets 0.9 — the second bucket sits beside his 0.4, showing hers weighs far more.

storyboard.claim: His wife weights proximity to her closest friends at 0.9.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same sorter gains a second bucket: Close friends: 0.9.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept sorter; her value added beside his.
storyboard.addedInformation: The contrast 0.4 vs 0.9 is visible side by side.

explainedBy: Next step: the two scenarios, A stay in Brooklyn and B move to California, are graded against those weighted values.

storyboard.claim: Then grade Option A (Brooklyn) and Option B (California) against the weighted values.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter with two options: A: Stay in Brooklyn, B: Move to California.
storyboard.onScreenText: A: Stay in Brooklyn / B: Move to California
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the values to the options they grade.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the two scenarios being scored.

explainedBy: The grading result: California scores high on nature but zero on the 0.9 friendship value — the third label shows the zero.

storyboard.claim: California scores high on nature but zero on the heavily weighted friendship value.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The options sorter gains: California: 0 on friends.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept sorter; the decisive score added.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows where Option B fails.

explainedBy: The arithmetic: multiply each score by its weight, add them up, and the scenario with the highest total wins.

storyboard.claim: Multiply, add up, and pick the scenario with the highest total value score.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: Multiply the scores -> Add them up -> Highest total.
storyboard.onScreenText: Multiply the scores / Add them up / Highest total
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Finishes the method after the grading.
storyboard.addedInformation: The final calculation steps; the turn to a work-life example is carried next beat.

explainedBy: The dilemma's first side: the listener, briefcase in hand, is offered a promotion that pays 40% more — literal money for his family's security.

storyboard.claim: You are offered a big promotion paying 40% more, securing your family's finances.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener with a briefcase, happy, beside a coin.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: New example: the work-life balance choice.
storyboard.addedInformation: The pay rise is concrete money.

explainedBy: The weighing: constant travel takes him from bedtimes and games, so he must weigh financial security against daily presence as a parent — the scale shows two sides.

storyboard.claim: The job's travel pulls you from your kids, so you weigh security against presence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same listener, now worried and slumped, beside a balance scale.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept listener; the coin becomes a scale and the face turns worried.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two sides of the trade-off.

explainedBy: Reaction: the host gets actively frustrated — weighing this with numbers feels psychopathic.
noVisual: A reaction; the angry face carries it.

storyboard.claim: The host is frustrated: this feels completely psychopathic.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener talking angrily.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the dilemma to an angry objection to the method.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the anger is the point.

explainedBy: The objection: you cannot put a decimal on missing friends or tucking a child in and run it through a spreadsheet — he holds the scoring sheet and rejects it.

storyboard.claim: You cannot score friends or bedtime and run it through a spreadsheet against stock options.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same angry listener now holds the scoring sheet; the spreadsheet phrase is struck.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept listener; he now holds the sheet he objects to.
storyboard.addedInformation: The rejected act: scoring love with numbers.

explainedBy: Why it hurts: the method strips the humanity and emotion out of a human choice — he slumps over the cold sheet.
noVisual: A feeling about the method; the slumped figure with the sheet carries it.

storyboard.claim: It is robotic and cold; it strips the humanity out of a human choice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener sad and slumped, still holding the sheet.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept listener; anger turns to sadness.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: names the coldness.

explainedBy: Concession: the other host agrees the exact decimals are absurd, a fiction — the author concedes to the frustrated listener, who is surprised.
noVisual: A concession in dialogue; the two faces carry it.

storyboard.claim: The co-host agrees: the specific decimal points are absurd, a fiction.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Johnson talks with a wry smile to the surprised listener.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the objection to an agreeing answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the concession is in the words.

explainedBy: Johnson's point: the final number matters least; the value is in the couple sitting down together over the value sheet.

storyboard.claim: Johnson argues the final score is the least important part; the value is in the process of sitting down.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Johnson sits at the kitchen table with the value sheet, his wife beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the couple from the method critique.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the act of sitting down together with the sheet.

explainedBy: The moment of insight: mapping their conflicting values openly with numbers, both of them realize something.

storyboard.claim: Mapping their values explicitly, Johnson and his wife realized something profound.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same couple at the table, both faces now surprised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; both faces change to surprise.
storyboard.addedInformation: The realization lands on both.

callout.text: Stay or go could never work

explainedBy: What they realized: a binary stay-or-go choice could never work, because each side gives up a highly weighted value.

storyboard.claim: A binary stay-or-go choice was never going to work with mutually exclusive values.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter of the binary: Stay in Brooklyn | Go to California.
storyboard.onScreenText: Stay in Brooklyn / Go to California
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The content of the realization.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the binary as two boxes.

explainedBy: Why the binary fails: Brooklyn can never offer year-round hiking and California can never replace 20-year friendships — each side loses something.

storyboard.claim: Brooklyn can't offer year-round hiking; California can't replicate a 20-year friendship.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The binary sorter gains what each side lacks.
storyboard.onScreenText: Brooklyn: no hiking / California: no old friends
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept sorter; the loss under each option added.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows each option sacrificing one value.

explainedBy: The tension breaks: Johnson points to a third, undiscovered path that honors both sets of values — the fork with a road straight ahead.

storyboard.claim: Seeing the weights on paper, they realized they needed a third path honoring both values.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Johnson points at a fork in the road with a third path straight ahead; his wife looks surprised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the two-box binary to a third path.
storyboard.addedInformation: The third option is drawn as a road.

explainedBy: Option C made concrete: they rent out the Brooklyn home and move to California for exactly two years as a bounded experiment — Johnson sets off down the third path.

storyboard.claim: Option C: rent out Brooklyn, move to California for exactly two years as an experiment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same fork; Johnson now walks onto the third path.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; pointing becomes walking.
storyboard.addedInformation: The bounded experiment.

explainedBy: The promise and the result: a promise to return if she was miserable, then a bicoastal life with roots in both places — now she walks the path too, both content.

storyboard.claim: With a promise to move back if she was miserable, they ended up bicoastal with roots in both places.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same fork; the wife now leads, both happy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the wife joins and both faces turn happy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her consent and the bicoastal outcome.

explainedBy: The lesson of the model: not a magic number, but the clarity to invent a new path — Johnson holds the value sheet that led them to the third road.

storyboard.claim: The model gave no magic number; it gave clarity to invent a new path.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same fork; Johnson now holds the value sheet.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the sheet reappears in his hand.
storyboard.addedInformation: Links the sheet to the new path.

callout.text: Let the conflict invent option C

explainedBy: The takeaway for the listener: when values conflict, don't force a binary — widen the map until a third path appears.

storyboard.claim: When values are irreconcilable, don't force a binary; widen the map first.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener points at the third path past the fork.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the couple's story to the listener's lesson.
storyboard.addedInformation: The general rule.

explainedBy: Turn: even with all the modeling, some things defy it — the listener's sheet of numbers is not enough.
noVisual: A transition line; the slumped figure with the sheet carries the limit.

storyboard.claim: Even with all the modeling in the world, some things defy it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener worried and slumped, holding his sheet.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transition to the final section.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: sets up the limit.

explainedBy: For truly unquantifiable decisions the hosts take us to a 19th-century writing desk — a Victorian novelist seated at work.

storyboard.claim: To explore unquantifiable decisions, go to a 19th-century writing desk.
storyboard.concreteVisual: George Eliot seated at her desk with pages.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the modern listener to the Victorian desk.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the era and place.

explainedBy: The novelist George Eliot scratches away with her pen, crafting her masterpiece — she writes at the desk.

storyboard.claim: George Eliot sits writing her masterpiece.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same desk; Eliot now absorbed and pleased in her writing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; she is named and her face changes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the novelist.

explainedBy: The work: the novel Middlemarch, one of the greatest psychological novels — the book appears beside her.

storyboard.claim: The novel is Middlemarch, one of the greatest psychological novels.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same desk; a book appears beside Eliot.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; the novel itself enters.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the book.

explainedBy: What she is doing, in scholars' terms: exploring narrativeness — working through a choice inside a story; she now holds the book.
noVisual: An academic term; the book and the callout carry it.

storyboard.claim: Scholars call what she is doing exploring narrativeness.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Eliot now holds the book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; she lifts the book instead of writing.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the term is text-carried.

explainedBy: The novel's choice: the passionate young Dorothea agonizes over whether to marry the dry old scholar Casaubon, who stands by blank, book in hand.

storyboard.claim: Eliot puts Dorothea through the agonizing choice of whether to marry Casaubon.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young Dorothea worried beside the gaunt, blank-faced Casaubon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the author to her characters.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two people in the choice and their contrast.

explainedBy: Eliot shows rigid calculation breaking against messy emotion: Dorothea's sadness against Casaubon's blankness.
noVisual: The breaking of a calculation is abstract; the two faces carry the human side.

storyboard.claim: Eliot shows how utilitarian calculus shatters on messy human emotion.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same pair; Dorothea now sad, Casaubon still blank.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; her face turns from worry to sadness.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the idea is text-carried.

explainedBy: The reason: some variables simply cannot be weighted on a spreadsheet — the spreadsheet phrase is rejected while Dorothea's fear stands.
noVisual: A negated claim; the struck phrase and the face carry it.

storyboard.claim: Some variables cannot be weighted on a spreadsheet.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same pair; Dorothea afraid; the spreadsheet phrase struck through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; her face changes again.
storyboard.addedInformation: The rejected method.

explainedBy: Callback: the fish suffocating under the algae bloom in Meadow Lake were living stakeholders — the lake itself on screen.

storyboard.claim: The fish suffocating in Meadow Lake were stakeholders in the planning decision.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The lake water on the shore, nobody on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the novel back to an earlier case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Recalls the lake.

explainedBy: The unanswerable question: how do you put a 0-to-1 weight on the survival of a fish or a forest — you can't.
noVisual: The impossibility is in the words; the tree shows the thing that resists weighting.

storyboard.claim: You can't put a decimal weight on the survival of a fish or a forest.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A tree in a forest.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the lake to living things in general.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the forest names the thing; the impossibility stays text.

explainedBy: An everyday choice with no math: how to care for an aging parent whose mind is declining — the listener slumps over the phone call.
noVisual: No icon reads as an aging parent; the worried listener and the callout carry it.

storyboard.claim: Think of the agonizing choice of how to care for an aging parent.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener at the kitchen table, worried, holding his phone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From nature to everyday human decisions.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the parent is not drawn.

explainedBy: Another such choice: whether to undergo a risky experimental medical treatment — the listener faces the medical sign, afraid.

storyboard.claim: Or whether to undergo a risky treatment that may extend life but ruin its quality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener, afraid, beside a medical cross.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second example of an unquantifiable choice.
storyboard.addedInformation: The medical setting.

explainedBy: In those moments a pros-and-cons list feels hollow, almost insulting — the list beside a dejected listener, not a helpful one.

storyboard.claim: A pro-con list or value model will feel hollow, almost insulting, in such choices.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The pros-and-cons list beside the sad, slumped listener.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the examples to the tool failing them.
storyboard.addedInformation: The list named by the narration is shown and rejected by the face.

explainedBy: Recap of the hour: the 3D intelligence model of the compound and cognitive diversity — the model itself on screen.

storyboard.claim: After an hour of 3D intelligence models and cognitive diversity...
storyboard.concreteVisual: The walled compound scale model on its table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The pushback begins by listing the tools discussed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Recalls the CIA model.

explainedBy: The pushback: after mock juries and Franklin, the ultimate tool is to read a Victorian novel? The listener holds up the book, surprised.

storyboard.claim: After all of that, the ultimate tool is reading a Victorian novel?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener holds a book, surprised.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the tools to the surprising recommendation.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book in hand is the tool named.

explainedBy: The answer: realist fiction is a rehearsal space for choices we only make once — the listener sits down to read.

storyboard.claim: Immersive realist fiction is a cognitive rehearsal space for once-in-a-life choices.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener seated, reading a book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From surprise to reading.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows reading as the practice.

explainedBy: Why it matters: you cannot practice caring for an aging parent or deciding to marry in real life — his face turns to worry over the book.
noVisual: The point is about real life having no practice runs; the face carries the weight.

storyboard.claim: You cannot practice caring for a parent or deciding to marry.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same reader, now worried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; face changes to worry.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the examples are text-carried.

explainedBy: You get one shot in life, but reading Middlemarch lets the brain simulate those choices — a rehearsal; his face lights up.

storyboard.claim: Reading Middlemarch, your brain simulates those choices: a rehearsal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same reader, now surprised and engaged.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; worry turns to discovery.
storyboard.addedInformation: The rehearsal idea.

explainedBy: Fiction as a flight simulator for the moral imagination, scaling up empathy — the reader, content, keeps reading.
noVisual: No vocabulary icon reads as a simulator or empathy; the reader and the callout carry it.

storyboard.claim: It acts as a flight simulator for the moral imagination and scales empathy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same reader, now happy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept stage; face turns happy.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the metaphor is text-carried.

explainedBy: The far-sighted global choices that need it: combating climate change, deciding whether to broadcast messages to the stars.

storyboard.claim: Civilization's far-sighted choices: climate change, messages to the stars, infrastructure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter of global choices: Global climate change | Messages to the stars.
storyboard.onScreenText: Global climate change / Messages to the stars
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From personal reading to civilization's choices.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the global decisions.

explainedBy: The problem these share: they affect people not born for 200 years, who are not in the room to vote — the third bucket names them.

storyboard.claim: Infrastructure choices affect people not born for 200 years, who can't vote in the room.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The sorter gains: Not born for 200 years.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept sorter; the absent stakeholders added.
storyboard.addedInformation: Who is affected but absent.

explainedBy: Empathy from narrative lets us simulate future people and advocate for them — the reader with his book before the widened map's third path.

storyboard.claim: Empathy generated by narrative is the ultimate tool to widen the map before choosing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The listener holding a book beside the fork with a third path.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Ties the book back to the widened-map idea.
storyboard.addedInformation: Links reading to the third path.

explainedBy: Empathy is the capstone of far-sightedness — then the host signals one last honest pushback; the reader still holds the book.
noVisual: A summary line; the kept reader and the callout carry it.

storyboard.claim: It is the capstone of far-sightedness; now one honest pushback on the whole premise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same listener with his book; the fork icon is gone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Kept listener; the callout names the conclusion.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the pushback starts next beat.
